title: Thiobarbituric acid-mediated chitosan–copper oxide nanozyme for ultrasensitive caffeic acid sensing and multimodal bioactivity
content: Caffeic acid is a dietary polyphenol valued for its antioxidant activity. However, it is also classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer as a Group 2B carcinogen. This motivates the need for sensitive, low-cost detection platforms. Here, we synthesized chitosan-coated copper oxide nanoparticles (Cs-CuO NPs) by a thiobarbituric acid-mediated method. This reagent has not been used to synthesize copper oxide nanoparticles. UV-Vis, FTIR, XRD, SEM-EDS, and TEM confirmed the formation of monoclinic CuO nanoparticles. Crystallite size was calculated to be 8.7 ± 0.6 nm by the Scherrer equation. The nanoparticles were uniformly stabilized within a chitosan matrix through Cu–N coordination. The nanocomposite showed strong peroxidase-mimicking activity. It was used to fabricate a signal-off colorimetric assay: caffeic acid selectively suppresses TMB/H2O2-generated absorbance. The assay gave a linear range of 0.01–60 µM, a detection limit of 1.9 nM, and a 60 s response time, outperforming several recently reported nanozyme-based sensors. It also selectively detected and quantified caffeic acid in the presence of structurally related interferents and retained activity in coffee, tea, and mint samples, confirming applicability to real samples. In addition to sensing, preliminary in vitro biological screening showed growth-inhibitory activity against Escherichia coli (25 mm) and Staphylococcus aureus (23 mm) in an agar well-diffusion assay. The nano-composite also demonstrated 88.9% DPPH radical-scavenging activity and nearly 91% inhibition of heat-induced albumin denaturation under the experimental conditions studied. These results provide preliminary evidence of complementary functional attributes that require systematic validation in biological systems. In conclusion, the developed nanozyme is a promising material for ultrasensitive detection of caffeic acid, and further study of its exploratory activity would be an interesting prospect for future research.
